trace: I am evaluating a 6-month momentum strategy selecting the top 75 stocks by price performance, rebalanced quarterly. The headline Sharpe of 0.95 over 15 years looks decent, but the collapse to 0.25 over the last 3 years is the core puzzle I need to explain. Attribution analysis is the right lens here. Momentum strategies load heavily on the UMD factor, and this one is no different: UMD explains 71% of excess returns. But the negative HML exposure at -0.38 and positive SMB tilt at 0.29 are working against the strategy in value-rotational environments, which have characterized recent markets. The alpha t-stat of 2.58 over the full period clears significance at the 1% level, but the deflated Sharpe of 0.68, a 28% reduction, reveals meaningful data mining bias embedded in the backtest. More damning, the last 3-year alpha t-stat is just 0.45, which is statistically indistinguishable from zero. That tells me the recent breakdown is not noise but structural. The real culprit is momentum crash dynamics: in the 8% of backtest observations characterized by sharp reversals after bull runs, the strategy bled -18.5% annualized. The past three years have looked exactly like a prolonged version of that regime. The static 6-month lookback is another vulnerability: it captures short-term noise and is highly sensitive to parameterization. A dual-momentum approach blending 6- and 12-month signals improves walk-forward Sharpe by 0.15. The 75-stock portfolio dilutes the pure momentum signal; trimming to 40-50 stocks pushes the information ratio from 0.45 to 0.58. Realistic transaction costs of 15 bps per trade at 120% annual turnover reduce the long-term Sharpe from 0.95 to 0.77, widening the implementation gap. The path forward is residual momentum, quality filtering to avoid junk momentum, and volatility scaling, projected to bring Sharpe to 1.20 with 30% lower max drawdown.

This 9-month momentum strategy on Russell 1000 stocks presents a similar but distinct profile to generic momentum models. The 15-year Sharpe of 1.15 is strong, but the fall to 0.30 over three years demands a proper post-mortem. Factor attribution is the starting point: UMD accounts for 55% of total returns, with secondary contributions from SMB at 11% and a growth tilt at 8%. The persistent negative Quality factor exposure of -0.21 is a structural weakness that has become material recently, as quality-neutral or quality-tilted strategies held up far better in the choppy post-2019 environment. The full-period alpha of 2.8% annualized with a t-stat of 2.95 and p-value of 0.003 confirms genuine historical edge. However, the deflated Sharpe of 0.89, a 22.6% haircut, signals that the 9-month lookback period is partially optimized to the in-sample window. Walk-forward analysis confirms this: a 6-month lookback would have outperformed by 4.5% annually in the last 3 years, indicating that the momentum cycle length has shifted. The regime dependency is stark: annualized alpha of +5.5% in low-volatility trending markets versus -8.2% in high-VIX environments. Monthly rebalancing adds 150% more turnover for only a 0.05 Sharpe gain, clearly not worth it, while semi-annual rebalancing causes meaningful signal decay of -0.28 Sharpe. The 75-stock universe allows junk names to drag the quality-adjusted signal. Recommended fixes are a quality factor overlay adding +0.25 Sharpe, dynamic VIX-based volatility scaling adding +0.20, and a residual momentum signal isolated from size and value adding +0.15. The strategy is salvageable but requires moving beyond a static, single-signal design.

The low P/B value strategy selecting the top 75 US large-cap stocks, rebalanced semi-annually, shows a Sharpe of 0.90 over 15 years but has deteriorated to -0.20 in the last 3 years, a complete reversal that is more alarming than a simple decline. Factor attribution explains most of it: 71% of historical returns trace back to factor exposures, primarily the Value (HML) factor at 55% and Size at 11%, with a negative Momentum drag of 8%. The unexplained alpha is modest, just 29% of returns, with a t-stat of 2.15 significant at 95% confidence, but the 3-year alpha t-stat has flipped negative to -1.88. The HML factor contributed -9.2% annually to performance over the recent window; combine that with -4.1% from the negative Momentum exposure and the arithmetic of poor performance becomes obvious. Sector concentration is a major amplifier: persistent overweights in Financials and Energy drove 45% of historical returns but account for 70% of the recent drawdown, a classic risk concentration masquerading as diversification. Walk-forward validation shows 35% Sharpe decay, and Bailey PBO estimate of 31% indicates moderate-to-high overfitting risk. The semi-annual rebalancing is too slow for a factor with drift characteristics, and the P/B metric itself is outdated: it ignores intangible assets and is mechanically biased toward capital-intensive industries like Financials. Optimal portfolio size appears to be around 60 stocks rather than 75, which dilutes factor exposure by 18% relative to a tighter 50-stock portfolio. Projected improvements: multi-factor integration with Quality adds +0.25 Sharpe, sector neutralization adds +0.15 Sharpe with 20% drawdown reduction, and dynamic rebalancing adds another +0.09 Sharpe.

The Mean Reversion Pairs Trading Strategy (MRPTS) on US Large-Cap Equities presents a textbook overfitting case: Sharpe of 1.80 in-sample over 2010-2018 collapsing to 0.30 out-of-sample from 2019-2023. The magnitude of degradation, an 83% Sharpe reduction, is the first red flag that this is not merely regime change but structural model failure. The deflated Sharpe of 0.65 after accounting for parameter selection bias is statistically insignificant, confirming that the in-sample performance was inflated by data mining. Bailey haircut of 48% and a CSCV overfitting probability of 65% make the diagnosis clear. The core flaw is pair selection via Pearson correlation rather than rigorous cointegration testing. Correlation captures co-movement but not the stable equilibrium relationship pairs trading requires. Out-of-sample, 72% of the top-correlated pairs failed to exhibit mean-reverting spreads; those relationships were spurious. The entry/exit threshold parameters of 2.0 and 0.5 standard deviations are highly curve-fitted: shifting the entry to 2.2 SD drops in-sample Sharpe by 0.50, which is characteristic of parameter optimization noise rather than genuine signal. The 252-day correlation lookback was optimal only for the 2010-2018 low-volatility, stable-correlation regime. Post-2019 brought macro-driven de-correlation and high-volatility regimes that destroyed pair stability. Unintended factor exposures to Momentum and Value became primary performance detractors in the out-of-sample window. The recommended overhaul is replacing Pearson correlation with Johansen cointegration tests for pair selection, implementing a VIX-based regime filter, enforcing factor neutrality constraints, and using walk-forward optimization to avoid static parameter lock-in. These changes address the root cause rather than patching symptoms.

This simple value strategy selecting the bottom 50 stocks by P/B from the S&P 500, rebalanced quarterly, carries a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 that has turned to -0.20 over the last 5 years. Unlike the momentum strategies in this dataset, the issue here is not overfitting: with few parameters and straightforward construction, Bailey overfitting probability is just 5%. The problem is a decaying factor premium. Factor attribution tells the story: HML explains 75% of variance, and HML has delivered persistently negative returns over the recent window, contributing -85% of the underperformance. The strategy also carries a -0.45 Momentum exposure that cost it during the momentum-driven bull market, accounting for -15% of the recent drag. The remaining -25% comes from the sector bet, a persistent underweight to mega-cap Technology of -22% combined with overweights to Financials (+18%) and Energy (+12%), structural overweights baked into P/B methodology rather than active choices. Alpha over the full period is just 0.25% annualized with a t-stat of 0.45, essentially zero, meaning the strategy never had standalone alpha and was purely a factor vehicle. Walk-forward Sharpe decay of 40% shows poor robustness to changing factor regimes. The optimal portfolio size is 30-40 stocks rather than 50, as expanding to 50 dilutes factor exposure by 18% and costs 0.12 Sharpe. Quarterly rebalancing is appropriate for this slow-moving factor: semi-annual would improve Sharpe by only 0.04 and monthly adds excessive turnover. The biggest bang for improvement is replacing P/B with a composite value metric adding +0.35 Sharpe, adding a quality screen adding +0.30, and sector neutralization adding +0.25.

This is another 6-month momentum strategy selecting the top 75 stocks, rebalanced quarterly, with the same 0.95 Sharpe over 15 years but now with an unspecified recent Sharpe that has deteriorated. The attribution picture looks familiar: UMD drives 71% of variance, with a small-cap tilt (SMB at 11%) as the secondary driver. Alpha net of factors is 0.9% annualized with a t-stat of 2.1, clearing the 95% significance bar over the full period. But the deflated Sharpe tells a more honest story: the 0.95 reported figure reduces to 0.71 after applying Bailey CSCV correction, a 25% inflation due to data mining. Out-of-sample validation confirms 40% performance decay, signaling fragility. In stable trending markets, this strategy shines with a Sharpe of 1.45, but it gets punished severely during momentum crashes, underperforming benchmark by over 15% in a single quarter during events like Q2 2009 or Q4 2018. The quarterly rebalancing cycle is too slow to react to sharp reversals; a shift to monthly rebalancing could reduce average drawdown duration by 45 days and improve the Sortino ratio by 0.20 even net of higher costs. Portfolio concentration also matters: 40-50 stocks increases momentum factor exposure by 12% and delivers a 0.11 higher Sharpe versus the current 75-stock diluted portfolio. The 6-month lookback has shortened to a 3-4 month optimal window in recent years as momentum cycles have compressed. The core recommendations are to shorten the lookback, increase rebalancing frequency, add a quality/low-volatility filter to avoid speculative momentum names, and neutralize sector bets to remove uncompensated risk. These structural fixes address the real drivers of recent deterioration.

This 9-month momentum strategy on Russell 1000 names with a 15-year Sharpe of 1.10, deteriorating to 0.35 recently, gives me another chance to isolate what distinguishes performing momentum variants from struggling ones. Factor decomposition: UMD explains 55% of returns, SMB explains 11%, and the remaining 29% is statistically significant alpha with a t-stat of 2.95. That is a cleaner signal than many variants. But the out-of-sample retention rate of just 55% of in-sample Sharpe, combined with a PBO of 31%, raises genuine concern that the 9-month lookback was over-optimized. The recent 3-year deterioration is primarily attributable to a negative momentum premium of -4.5% annualized, which alone accounts for -68% of attributional impact. The strategy suffered a momentum crash regime as factor volatility spiked and crowding unwound. Sensitivity analysis is instructive: a 6-month lookback would have outperformed by 45% over the last 3 years, showing the cycle length has shortened. Quarterly rebalancing is suboptimal 35% of the time during high-volatility periods; a bi-monthly cadence in volatile regimes could capture an additional 1.2% annualized net of costs. The 75-stock equal-weight design creates crowding risk; expanding to 150 stocks with risk-parity weighting improves the information ratio from 0.88 to 1.05. At 65% quarterly turnover with 10 bps slippage, the annual drag is 2.6%, which realistic market impact estimates would push higher. The recommended improvements are a dynamic momentum signal incorporating residual momentum, a volatility-scaling overlay, and a QMJ quality filter, projected to lift the long-term Sharpe to 1.45 with 25% better drawdown characteristics.

The low P/B strategy selecting the bottom quintile of the Russell 1000, rebalanced quarterly over 2008-2023, carries a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 but has generated negative alpha in the last 3 years. This is a pure factor vehicle: HML explains 71% of returns, and the strategy carries a negative Momentum exposure of -0.41 and a negative Quality exposure of -0.25, both of which are structural liabilities in growth-and-momentum-dominated markets. The 15-year alpha t-stat of 1.98 is barely significant at the 5% level, and excluding the 2009 recovery period renders it statistically insignificant entirely, which is a meaningful fragility test. Recent 3-year alpha is -2.1% annually. The primary drag is the negative value factor premium over that window at -4.5% contribution to relative performance. Value traps are an acute secondary problem: low P/B stocks that are cheap for fundamental reasons, distress or declining earnings, contributed 65% of the negative returns over the last 3 years. The negative Momentum exposure is the tertiary culprit as high-momentum stocks powered the market. Overfitting risk is low given the strategy simplicity, but factor crowding and decay are real concerns. Quarterly rebalancing is actually too frequent here; semi-annual would reduce turnover by 40% with only 0.02 Sharpe cost, and the bottom decile rather than quintile captures purer factor exposure. Quality filter with ROIC greater than 10% is the most impactful fix at +0.20 Sharpe, adding a momentum screen to exclude the bottom decile of 12-month momentum adds +0.15, and sector neutralization reduces Financials and Energy concentration for +0.10 Sharpe.

The low-volatility strategy selecting the bottom 100 stocks by 252-day realized volatility, rebalanced quarterly, delivered a 15-year Sharpe of 0.95 before showing negative alpha of -1.8% annually in the last 3 years. Attribution points to primary exposure to the BAB (Betting Against Beta) and QMJ (Quality Minus Junk) factors as the historical performance drivers. The recent breakdown traces to a junk rally regime where defensive positioning was penalized as low-quality, high-beta stocks surged and risk premia compressed. The full-period alpha of 1.5% annualized with a t-stat of 2.51 and p-value of 0.012 is statistically significant at the 98% level, but the deflated Sharpe of 0.79 reflects moderate overfitting. Transaction cost impact is meaningful but manageable: 45% annual turnover at 20 bps per trade generates 0.18% annual drag, reducing Sharpe from 0.95 to 0.90, with an additional 0.04% from market impact on large-cap low-vol names. Parameter sensitivity is relatively low: a 10% change in the 252-day lookback costs only 0.04 Sharpe on average. Portfolio size matters more: trimming to 50 stocks increases Sharpe to 1.02 but raises drawdown, while expanding to 200 stocks dilutes the factor to 0.88 Sharpe. Monthly rebalancing adds 250% turnover for a negligible 0.02 gross Sharpe improvement that disappears net of costs; semi-annual causes 0.11 Sharpe decay from factor drift. The key vulnerability is momentum: momentum crashes hit this strategy disproportionately because low-vol names become crowded and unwind violently. Integrating value and momentum filters to build a multi-style defensive portfolio is projected to improve Sharpe by 0.25 and reduce drawdown by 20%.

The small-cap momentum strategy on the Russell 2000, selecting the top 75 stocks by 9-month performance, rebalanced quarterly, shows a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 that has collapsed to -0.20 recently. This is the worst deterioration I have seen in this dataset so far, and the small-cap dimension explains much of it. Factor attribution: UMD and SMB collectively explain 71% of variance. Negative Quality exposure reveals a structural preference for low-quality, high-beta small caps, which were brutal in the flight-to-quality environment of recent years. Long-term alpha t-stat of 2.15 with p-value of 0.031 is technically significant, but 3-year rolling alpha has held below a t-stat of 1.0 for 36 consecutive months, erasing any inference about current edge. The deflated Sharpe of just 0.55 after selection bias correction reveals substantial overfitting, and the 9-month lookback sits near a sharp performance peak with a 0.22 average Sharpe decline from any deviation, a classic sign of parameter fitting to historical data. Transaction costs are the most severe issue unique to this small-cap implementation: 310% annual turnover at a conservative 50 bps per trade generates a 3.1% annual performance drag, which alone is enough to kill the strategy in low-return environments. The three causes of the -0.20 Sharpe are the momentum factor itself at -9.5% contribution, the rotation away from small caps at -6.8%, and the quality tilt in a quality-favoring market at -4.2%. Semi-annual rebalancing would cut turnover by 45% and improve Sharpe by 0.11. Expanding the portfolio to 150 stocks improves the information ratio by 0.15 through better diversification. Adding a quality/low-volatility filter and residual momentum signal to neutralize unintended factor bets is projected to bring the robust Sharpe to approximately 1.10.

The QARP (Quality-at-a-Reasonable-Price) US Equities Strategy delivers a 12-year Sharpe of 1.35, and I want to understand exactly which factors explain that and where unintended bets are hiding. The composite score weighting is 60% quality metrics (ROE, D/E, earnings stability) and 40% value metrics (P/E, P/B, FCF yield), rebalanced quarterly from the Russell 1000. Factor attribution breaks out as: Quality at 45% of returns, Value at 22%, and Market Beta slightly below 1.0 contributing 11%, totaling 78% factor-explained. The remaining 22% is unexplained alpha with a t-stat of 3.12, significant at the 99.8% level, indicating genuine stock selection skill rather than pure factor harvesting. The most consequential unintended bet is a persistent negative Momentum exposure of -0.25 on average, detracting 5% from total returns over the period. During momentum-led rallies, this drag is particularly acute. There is also a minor positive Low Volatility loading of 0.15. The Value exposure is the dynamic one: it has decayed roughly 20% over the last 5 years as quality companies have seen multiple expansion, compressing the valuation signal in the composite score. The factor-adjusted Sharpe of 0.95 after neutralizing primary factor exposures confirms the alpha contribution is real. Semi-annual rebalancing would cut turnover by 45% with only a 0.04 Sharpe cost, suggesting current quarterly frequency is slightly excessive. The most impactful fix is a momentum screen to filter out the lowest momentum quintile, projected to add 0.15 Sharpe. Replacing P/B with EV/EBITDA in the composite improves the value factor beta from 0.38 to 0.45 for an additional 0.07 Sharpe. The Information Ratio of 0.88 validates the active management quality.

The Deep Value strategy selecting the bottom 5% of Russell 1000 stocks by P/B ratio, rebalanced quarterly, shows a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 but a negative Sharpe of -0.20 in the last 3 years. This is an extreme deterioration that warrants a diagnosis of structural failure rather than a cyclical patch. Historical attribution is stark: a 0.78 beta to HML explains 85% of excess returns, and alpha generation was statistically insignificant at a t-stat of just 0.8. This strategy never had genuine stock-picking edge; it was pure factor exposure. And that factor has been in sustained drawdown, contributing -6.5% annually to returns over the last 3 years. The compounding problem is a persistent negative Momentum exposure of -0.45, because systematically buying the cheapest stocks means buying recent losers. In a trending market, that is a structural headwind. Walk-forward analysis shows 90% performance decay in the most recent out-of-sample period, indicating a structural break not a regime wobble. The P/B metric is the root cause: it is mechanically useless for intangible-asset-heavy companies, which now dominate the index, and systematically biases the portfolio toward troubled industries like Financials and Energy. The 0-5% quintile is full of value traps; the 6-10% quintile actually outperformed the deepest value by 2.2% annually over the last 5 years, a finding that argues against concentrating in the absolute cheapest names. The recommended overhaul is replacing single-metric P/B with a composite of P/E, FCF Yield, and EV/EBITDA, adding a quality filter removing the bottom 25% by ROE and D/E, and implementing a momentum filter. Composite changes are projected to bring 3-year Sharpe from -0.20 to +0.65.

The Small-Cap Value strategy selecting the bottom quintile by P/B from the Russell 2000, rebalanced quarterly over 15 years with a Sharpe of 0.85 and recent negative alpha, combines two factors that have both faced headwinds simultaneously. Attribution: SMB contributes 45% and HML 33% of excess returns, totaling 78% factor-explained. Modest alpha of 1.2% annualized with t-stat of 2.1 existed pre-2020 but has reversed sharply. The three-layer diagnosis of recent underperformance is: HML contributing -4.5% annually as the primary driver given the 0.85 beta to Value; value traps creating a negative Quality exposure of -0.25 that cost 1.8% annually as secondary driver; and the broader market regime favoring intangible-asset-heavy growth companies rendering P/B less effective as tertiary driver, with 65% of selected stocks underperforming the Russell 2000 index over the period. Overfitting risk is low given strategy simplicity, and parameter sensitivity analysis shows stable performance across rebalancing frequencies and quintile sizes. Quarterly rebalancing at 65% annual turnover generates 0.26% annual drag at 20 bps round-trip, which is manageable. A shift to monthly increases costs and reduces Sharpe by 0.12; semi-annual introduces 0.08 Sharpe decay from style drift. Portfolio concentration at the quintile level is appropriate; further concentration to the top 50 stocks within the quintile reduces Sharpe from 0.85 to 0.78. Optimization potential is high: integrating Quality and Momentum factors with a modernized composite value metric is projected to improve Sharpe by +0.35 and reduce max drawdown by 25%.

The 9-month momentum strategy selecting the top 75 stocks, rebalanced quarterly, with a best-in-class 15-year Sharpe of 1.35 that has dropped to 0.40 presents an interesting diagnostic challenge. The long history of outperformance suggests a real signal; the collapse demands explanation. Attribution: Momentum Beta of 0.88 explains 55% of returns, Size Beta of 0.25 explains 11%, and a substantial unexplained alpha of 4.5% annually with t-stat of 3.1 confirms genuine edge beyond factor harvesting. But the deflated Sharpe of 0.98 and a PBO of 28% suggest some of that apparent alpha was parameter selection luck. Out-of-sample validation on a separate 5-year period shows 60% Sharpe decay, which is significant. The recent 3-year breakdown traces to: negative momentum factor premium contributing -7.1% to performance; high exposure to volatility risk during the regime shift; and crowded positioning in high-growth, high-beta stocks that suffered disproportionately during the correction. The 9-month lookback creates vulnerability to sharp reversals: a 6-month lookback would have cut recent drawdown by 15% at a cost of 0.10 Sharpe long-term. The 75-stock portfolio dilutes the signal versus 40-50 stocks which show +0.12 Sharpe at +20% volatility. Quarterly rebalancing generates 65 bps annual drag from slippage, and realistic implementation shortfall would reduce historical Sharpe from 1.35 to 1.22. The path to improvement is signal blending with a 1-month reversal filter to mitigate crash risk, momentum quality overlay, dynamic volatility scaling, and sector-neutral construction, projected to produce an all-weather Sharpe of 1.10 with 30% lower max drawdown.

The Global Dividend Yield strategy investing in the top 100 highest-yielding stocks from the MSCI World Index, rebalanced quarterly over 12 years with a Sharpe of 0.85, is primarily a factor harvesting vehicle rather than an alpha generator. Factor attribution covers 78% of return variance: Value (HML) explains 45% of returns as the dominant intended driver, while negative Momentum exposure creates a -12% drag on performance. The unintended exposures are the most interesting part: a persistent negative Quality loading of -0.25 reveals systematic investment in lower-quality value traps, which has intensified from -0.15 to -0.32 over the last five years, coinciding with the period of underperformance. There is also a minor positive Low Volatility (BAB) loading of 0.18. The residual alpha is just 0.52% annualized with a t-stat of 0.98 and p-value of 0.33, statistically insignificant, confirming this is purely factor exposure rather than stock selection skill. The mechanism is direct: high dividend yields correlate with low valuation multiples (Value) but also with financial distress or poor growth prospects, which explains the negative Quality loading. The portfolio size choice matters: concentrating to 50 stocks intensifies the Value exposure but worsens Quality contamination; expanding to 200 dilutes all factor bets. The most impactful improvement is a quality screen requiring ROE above 10% and Debt/Equity below 1.0, projected to add 0.15 Sharpe and generate statistically significant alpha by reducing the negative quality drag. Sector weight caps at 20% would have prevented the 5% drawdown during the 2018 Financials downturn. Quarterly rebalancing is appropriate for this low-turnover style, but sector concentration risk from Financials and Utilities must be managed explicitly.

The S&P 500 low-volatility strategy selecting the 100 lowest-volatility stocks, rebalanced quarterly, shows a 15-year Sharpe of 0.90 but has ground to near zero at 0.10 over the last 3 years. Attribution reveals that 75% of historical excess returns are explained by the Fama-French 5-factor model plus the Low Volatility (BAB) factor, with a primary Beta of 0.68 to BAB and a secondary positive Quality exposure of 0.25. The strategy generated no statistically significant alpha: 0.2% annually with a t-stat of 0.45. This is a pure factor vehicle. The 3-year underperformance traces directly to interest rate sensitivity: low-volatility stocks behave like long-duration bonds, and the rising rate environment of the last 3 years contributed -4.5% to annual performance. The BAB factor itself provided only 0.5% premium, grossly insufficient to offset that headwind. The probability of outperforming in the current regime without modification is just 25%. Portfolio size analysis shows diminishing returns past 80 stocks: the marginal 20 stocks reduce BAB beta from 0.75 to 0.68 without meaningful diversification benefit. A 180-day lookback improves the information ratio by 0.10 with only a 15% cost increase versus the current 252-day. Quarterly rebalancing is suboptimal; a bi-monthly schedule captures an additional 0.8% net of transaction costs. Rebalancing at quarter-end coincides with index fund flows, adding 5 bps of avoidable market impact annually. The recommended evolution is toward a multi-factor, regime-aware model incorporating a value filter to offset duration risk and dynamic factor weighting based on the interest rate cycle, projected to bring Sharpe to 0.75 in the current environment.

The concentrated 6-month momentum strategy selecting only the top 30 stocks from the Russell 1000, rebalanced quarterly, with a 15-year Sharpe of 0.90 declining to 0.25 recently, is notable for its concentration risk. Thirty stocks is a very narrow portfolio for a momentum strategy; that choice amplifies factor purity but creates significant sector bets and idiosyncratic risk. Attribution: UMD explains 71% of historical excess returns historically, but this contribution has inverted to -45% over the last 3 years during the momentum crash environment. Unintended exposures include a Size tilt (SMB Beta 0.28) and a negative Value exposure (HML Beta -0.41). Long-term alpha t-stat of 2.25 (p=0.024) is significant, but significance disappears on recent data. The deflated Sharpe of 0.61 reflects a 32% inflation from data snooping, and the out-of-sample Sharpe decay is a severe 72%, suggesting material overfitting in the parameter choices. Transaction costs are a major drag unique to this implementation: 280% annual turnover at 15 bps effective cost creates 0.84% annual performance drag, and in the recent high-volatility environment, realistic slippage is closer to 20 bps, which would push that drag above 1%. The concentrated 30-stock portfolio amplifies the momentum crash problem: when high-momentum names reverse, there is no diversification buffer. Expanding to 50-75 stocks improves the information ratio by 18% through diversification while only slightly diluting the momentum signal. Semi-annual rebalancing cuts turnover 45% with only 7% gross alpha reduction, improving net Sharpe by 0.09. Dynamic signal blending with 12-month momentum and a volatility overlay is projected to lift Sharpe to 1.15 with 25% drawdown reduction.

The Global Low-Volatility Anomaly strategy investing in the lowest quintile by 180-day realized volatility across the MSCI World Index, rebalanced quarterly from 2005-2023 with a Sharpe of 0.85, is one of the more robust factor strategies I have analyzed here. Factor attribution shows 78% of excess returns explained by BAB and Quality factors collectively. Alpha of 1.1% annually with a t-stat of 2.10 is statistically significant at the 95% level, suggesting genuine incremental value beyond pure factor harvesting. The deflated Sharpe of 0.76, a haircut of just 10.6%, is the most encouraging robustness signal I have seen in this dataset, indicating low data mining bias. Walk-forward analysis retains 85% of in-sample Sharpe, and the parameter sensitivity grid shows a broad performance plateau around 150-200 day lookbacks with quarterly rebalancing, confirming the chosen parameters are not curve-fitted. Out-of-sample split testing (2005-2014 Sharpe 0.89, 2015-2023 Sharpe 0.81) shows good stability. The unintended exposures are a negative Momentum loading and a negative Size loading, which have worsened since 2018 and explain underperformance during momentum-led rallies. The lowest quintile yields roughly 250-300 stocks; concentrating to the lowest decile increases BAB Beta from 0.75 to 0.92 but reduces the information ratio from 0.45 to 0.38 due to higher idiosyncratic risk. A 120-day lookback improves responsiveness with 15% more turnover for a 0.05 Sharpe gain. Rebalancing in the second week of the month rather than quarter-end avoids 5-7 bps of annual index-driven market impact. Neutralizing unintended sector and country bets and adding a quality-score overlay are the primary improvement levers.

The Defensive Quality strategy selecting top quintile stocks on low leverage, high ROE, and stable earnings growth, rebalanced quarterly with a 15-year Sharpe of 0.95, is a textbook quality factor implementation. Attribution is clean: Quality (QMJ) explains 55% of excess returns and Low Volatility (BAB) explains 23%, together accounting for 78%. Alpha is statistically significant at a t-stat of 2.51 (p=0.012), confirming skill above and beyond factor harvesting. The most notable robustness signals in this dataset: Bailey haircut of just 8%, deflated Sharpe of 0.85, 5-fold cross-validation retaining 93% of in-sample Sharpe at 0.89, and a Monte Carlo 95% confidence interval of [0.72, 1.15] that firmly excludes zero. This is a genuinely robust strategy. The structural weakness is a persistent negative Momentum exposure of -0.35, which causes meaningful underperformance during momentum-led rallies, particularly in the post-2020 period when this strategy lagged. Average annual turnover of 22% is remarkably low, which explains both the low transaction cost profile and the slow adaptation to market dynamics that creates the momentum lag. The strategy is most sensitive to the ROE threshold parameter: a 1% increase improves Quality Beta by 0.08 but reduces diversification and raises idiosyncratic risk by 5%. Static equal weighting of the three quality metrics is suboptimal; dynamic weighting that overweights earnings stability in high-volatility regimes would improve the Sortino ratio by 10%. The one targeted fix that delivers the most return on effort is a momentum overlay or filter to neutralize the negative Momentum exposure, projected to add 0.15 Sharpe without compromising defensive characteristics.

The deep value strategy selecting the lowest 10% of Russell 1000 stocks by P/B ratio, rebalanced quarterly, carries a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 that has deteriorated significantly in the last 3 years. The attribution is similar to other low-P/B strategies I have reviewed but with the unique element of the lowest decile creating higher concentration in genuinely distressed names. HML explains 71% of excess returns, SMB adds 15%, and there is a -9% drag from negative Momentum exposure. Full-period alpha is 0.75% annualized with a t-stat of 2.10, marginally significant, but it has turned to -2.1% annualized recently. The regime analysis is clear: the strategy shines in economic recoveries and stable rising-rate environments (Sharpe 1.25) but struggles in growth-led bull markets (Sharpe 0.35 recently). Three-year performance drag comes from: HML premium at -6.5% annually as primary cause; negative Momentum costing -1.8% as secondary; and Technology underweight opportunity cost at -4.2% as tertiary. Overfitting risk is low given single-parameter simplicity, so the problem is pure factor cyclicality. Sensitivity testing of the threshold shows moving to the lowest 5% increases distressed-firm exposure and worsens the Sortino ratio by 0.18; expanding to 20% dilutes value beta by 18% but reduces tail risk. Monthly rebalancing adds 150% turnover for only 0.02 gross Sharpe improvement, confirming quarterly is near-optimal. The three improvements with highest projected impact: quality filter (ROE above 15%) adding +0.20 Sharpe to avoid value traps; Momentum neutralization adding +0.15; and sector-relative value scoring adding +0.12 Sharpe by eliminating the persistent Technology underweight.

The small-cap value strategy selecting the top 100 stocks by book-to-market ratio, rebalanced quarterly, shows a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 that has eroded to -0.10 recently. The attribution framework is by now familiar: Value (HML) at 45%, Size (SMB) at 25%, and Market Beta at 5% explain 75% of long-term returns. The remaining 25% is statistically significant alpha with a t-stat of 2.51 over the full period. But the strategy fails the White Reality Check on the recent 3-year window, meaning it is not robust across all market conditions. The recent deterioration has three drivers: negative value factor premium contributing -7.2% annual drag as the primary cause; negative Momentum exposure at -0.45 beta in a market rewarding momentum as secondary; and rising interest rate sensitivity as tertiary. Transaction costs are an acute problem in this implementation: 85% annual turnover in small-cap names generates 1.2% annual drag from slippage and commissions, eroding 25% of gross alpha. A VWAP execution algorithm over 3 days rather than same-day rebalancing could cut market impact costs by 30-40 bps annually. Portfolio concentration analysis shows the value premium is more potent in the top 50-75 names; expanding to 100 stocks dilutes factor exposure by 18% and adds lower-quality names. The B/M metric itself is a structural limitation: it is vulnerable to accounting manipulation and performs poorly for asset-light businesses. A composite value score using E/P, S/P, and FCF/EV reduces sector biases by 15% and improves consistency. The hybrid 2-month/quarterly dynamic rebalancing schedule improves the information ratio by 0.11 versus static quarterly. Quality filter integration is projected to add +0.25 Sharpe and cut max drawdown by 20%, with dynamic factor timing adding another +0.15.

The 6-month momentum strategy selecting the top 75 stocks, rebalanced quarterly, with a 15-year Sharpe of 1.10 declining to approximately 0.35 over the last 3 years, sits in the middle of the momentum performance range I have seen across this dataset. Attribution is standard: Momentum factor is the primary driver with secondary negative Value tilt. Alpha t-stat of 2.95 over the full period confirms genuine edge, though the deflated Sharpe of 0.88 indicates moderate overfitting risk. The 6-month lookback is the most sensitive parameter: walk-forward analysis shows a 3-month lookback would have improved recent Sharpe by 0.25, while 9-12 months would have worsened it, making this genuinely a worst-of-both-worlds lookback for the current rapid rotation environment. Quarterly rebalancing shows good cost-benefit balance: monthly adds 70 bps cost for only 0.05 Sharpe; semi-annual saves 40 bps but costs 0.15 Sharpe. Average turnover of 220% at 25 bps total transaction cost generates 55 bps annual drag, reducing gross Sharpe from 1.16 to the reported 1.10. Reducing portfolio from 75 to 50 stocks increases momentum exposure by 18% for +0.08 gross Sharpe but raises concentration risk. A dynamic lookback regime using 3-month lookback when VIX is above 25 and 9-month when below 15 is the highest-leverage improvement, projected to add 0.20 Sharpe. A quality filter to avoid low-quality momentum names combined with sector neutralization addresses the unintended factor exposure problem. Combined optimizations target a Sharpe of 1.45 with improved resilience in adverse regimes.

The low-volatility strategy selecting the bottom 100 S&P 500 stocks by 90-day realized volatility, rebalanced quarterly, carries a 15-year Sharpe of 0.95 but has underperformed its benchmark by 5% annually over the last 3 years. The attribution structure here is more alpha-rich than most low-vol strategies I have examined: BAB factor explains 55% of excess returns, Quality adds 15%, and negative Market Beta (-0.25) contributes 12%, with a statistically significant alpha of 1.8% annualized at a t-stat of 2.5 and p-value of 0.012 remaining after factor adjustment. Recent underperformance has three clear causes: 60% attributable to the bull market regime driven by high-beta, high-growth technology names, where the strategy negative beta and negative Momentum exposure of -0.30 were penalized; 25% from compressed volatility premium as the spread between high and low vol stocks narrowed; and 15% from the persistent Technology underweight of -15% versus benchmark. The probability of an extended drawdown lasting 3+ years is estimated at 18%, which is material. The 90-day lookback is actually the weakest parameter: a 120-180 day window provides more stable volatility estimates and improves Sharpe by 0.07 by reducing short-term noise capture. Transaction costs are minimal: 28% annual turnover at 20 bps generates just 20 bps drag, and market impact on large-cap liquid names is negligible at under 5 bps. Portfolio size at 100 stocks is near-optimal. The core enhancement path is a factor-neutral overlay controlling for negative Momentum and Market Beta exposures, supplemented by blending with a complementary Value signal to improve performance in growth-led rallies and a dynamic volatility target to adapt to regime changes.

The concentrated 9-month momentum strategy selecting only the top 30 stocks, rebalanced quarterly, with a 15-year Sharpe of 0.90 that has dropped to -0.20 recently represents the intersection of two risk amplifiers: concentrated portfolio and long momentum lookback. The primary attribution finding is that Momentum explains 71% of variance, but the remaining alpha is statistically insignificant at a t-stat of just 1.12, meaning this is almost entirely a pure factor vehicle with no stock selection edge. The 35% PBO estimate reflects moderate overfitting risk. Recent -0.20 Sharpe is driven by momentum crash dynamics: a high Beta of 1.15 and negative Low Volatility exposure of -0.45 both amplified losses when momentum reversed. The 30-stock concentration means there is zero diversification buffer during these crashes. Parameter sensitivity confirms the vulnerability: the 9-month lookback lacks robustness, with a 6-month period reducing recent drawdown by 20% and a 12-month period worsening it by 15%. Transaction costs at zero in the backtest need adjustment: 10 bps for slippage and commission at 120% annual turnover reduces long-term Sharpe from 0.90 to 0.78. The quarterly rebalancing creates a 4-6 week lag in adapting to new market leaders, contributing an estimated 1.5% to annual underperformance in high-rotation environments. Expanding to 50-75 stocks reduces volatility by 18% at a cost of 0.10 Sharpe. The most impactful algorithmic improvement is blending the pure price signal with fundamental momentum (earnings estimate revisions) in a 70/30 ratio, projected to increase the information ratio by 0.25. A momentum crash filter reducing market exposure when high-momentum and low-volatility stock correlations turn sharply negative is the risk management priority.

The 252-day low-volatility strategy selecting the bottom 100 stocks, rebalanced quarterly, with a 15-year Sharpe of 0.90 that has declined to 0.20 recently follows the familiar low-vol underperformance pattern but is notable for its clean parameter robustness. The deflated Sharpe of 0.82, a haircut of only 8.9%, is one of the better overfitting signals in this dataset, and performance is stable across lookback windows from 126 to 300 days with only 0.02 Sharpe loss per 50-day deviation. Factor attribution: Low Volatility (SMLV) explains 55% of returns as expected, but negative Value exposure (HML: -0.38) and negative Momentum (UMD: -0.25) are both structural drags that have intensified in the recent environment. Full-period alpha of 1.1% annualized at t-stat 2.1 has turned to -0.8% in the recent window. The three-layer diagnosis of recent deterioration: adverse factor environment with negative Value exposure generating -4.2% annual drag as primary cause; duration sensitivity of the portfolio averaging 4.5 years making it behave like a long bond in the rising-rate cycle as secondary; and sector concentration in Utilities and Consumer Staples at +15% versus benchmark hurting during tech-led rallies as tertiary. The strategy excels in risk-off periods (Sharpe 1.35) but delivers only 0.15 Sharpe in sharp recoveries and rising-rate environments. Semi-annual rebalancing analysis is warranted given the parameter stability. The three optimization levers are: quality and value filter for factor neutralization adding +0.25 Sharpe; dynamic volatility targeting replacing fixed stock count adding +0.15; and duration hedge overlay during rising rate environments adding +0.12 Sharpe.

The QARP strategy selecting top 75 stocks on a composite of ROE, D/E, and P/E, rebalanced quarterly from 2008-2023, shows a 15-year Sharpe of 0.95 that has deteriorated to 0.25 in the last 3 years. This is a genuine quality-value blend and the attribution reflects both factor contributions. Quality drives 45% of returns, Value drives 35%, and Low Volatility adds 10%, with a statistically significant alpha of 1.8% annualized at t-stat 2.58. The deflated Sharpe of 0.84 represents only an 11.6% haircut, confirming low data mining bias. The strategy is structurally sound over the long run. The recent collapse traces to three causes: the Value factor premium turning negative contributed -4.2% annual drag as the primary driver; the strategy negative Momentum exposure of -0.45 in a market rewarding high-momentum stocks was the secondary drag; and the quarterly rebalancing being too slow to adapt to rapid rotations in market leadership themes was the tertiary cause, creating a 1.2% performance lag versus a hypothetical monthly portfolio. The static 50/50 factor weighting is the core mechanical weakness: a 70/30 Quality/Value split would have improved the 15-year Sharpe to 1.05 and reduced recent drawdown by 15%, and walk-forward analysis shows the 50/50 split was suboptimal most of the time. Concentrating the portfolio to 40-50 stocks would improve Quality factor exposure and add approximately 0.09 Sharpe. The strategy outperforms meaningfully in stable sideways markets (+2.5% alpha) and recessions (+3.1% alpha), confirming genuine defensive value, but it systematically bleeds in growth-led bull markets (-2.8% alpha). Regime-adaptive weighting is the highest-value fix, projected to add +0.20 Sharpe, ahead of momentum overlay at +0.15 and replacing P/E with FCF yield at +0.12.

The Value-Momentum multi-factor strategy selecting the top quintile of US large-cap stocks on a 50/50 composite score, rebalanced quarterly from 2010-2023, shows a full-period Sharpe of 1.35 collapsing to 0.60 recently. The thesis behind this strategy was sound historically: Value and Momentum factors had a long-term correlation of -0.15, providing genuine diversification within the composite. The strategy generated 2.8% annualized alpha with a t-stat of 3.1 over the full period. But the Chow test for a structural break in late 2020 is positive, confirming this is a genuine regime shift, not sampling noise. The correlation between Value and Momentum spiked from -0.15 to +0.35 in the recent period, eliminating the diversification benefit that was the core architectural premise of the strategy. The Value factor has also underperformed simultaneously, creating a double headwind. The deflated Sharpe of 1.05 still shows some data snooping in the original design. The static 50/50 weighting is the critical mechanical weakness: walk-forward analysis shows it was suboptimal 65% of the time, and perfect foresight weighting could have achieved 1.90 Sharpe. The top quintile selection dilutes factor exposure by 18% versus the top decile, reducing Information Ratio from 0.85 to 0.70. Transaction costs of 95 bps annually from quarterly rebalancing could be reduced by 40 bps shifting to semi-annual with only a 0.05 Sharpe sacrifice. Executing trades over a 5-day window cuts market impact by 25 bps. The path to restoration is dynamic factor weighting based on rolling correlation and factor momentum, projected to bring Sharpe to 1.45 with 20% lower max drawdown.

The Global Quality-Value Fusion (QV-Fusion) strategy selecting the top quintile of MSCI World stocks on a 50/50 Quality-Value composite, rebalanced semi-annually from 2008-2023, delivers a Sharpe of 0.95 and annualized return of 11.2%. This is a genuinely international multi-factor strategy and the attribution is rich. Quality contributes 4.1% of the 11.2% return, Value contributes 2.8%, while a persistent negative Momentum exposure subtracts 1.5%. The strategy also shows a pro-cyclical Market Beta exposure creating drawdown risk during sharp downturns. Alpha of 2.1% annualized with t-stat of 2.58 confirms stock selection skill, but the alpha drops to 1.8% with t-stat 2.20 when Momentum is added to the factor model, revealing partial momentum omission bias. The deflated Sharpe of 0.81, a 14.7% haircut, indicates low-to-moderate overfitting risk. Walk-forward analysis retains 85% of in-sample Sharpe, and Monte Carlo projections show a 95% confidence interval of 7.5-14.5% annualized returns with 90% probability of benchmark outperformance. Semi-annual rebalancing is the primary mechanical inefficiency: shifting to quarterly would capture the value premium more accurately for a 65 bps annual performance improvement. A 60/40 Quality/Value tilt would have improved Sharpe to 1.05 by reducing volatility in stress periods. Regime analysis confirms the pattern: +4.5% alpha in risk-off flight-to-quality environments, -3.2% alpha in momentum-driven bull markets like 2017 and 2020. An unintended large-cap drift has diluted the size premium in the second half of the backtest. Neutralizing the Momentum exposure with a filter would address the most consistent drag.

The book-to-market value strategy selecting the top 75 stocks from the Russell 1000, rebalanced quarterly, shows a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 that has turned deeply negative at -0.20 over the last 5 years. This is one of the purest single-factor strategies in this dataset: 85% of return variance is explained by the HML factor, and the alpha is a statistically insignificant -0.5% with t-stat -0.45, confirming there is no stock selection edge at all. This is entirely a factor harvesting vehicle. Overfitting probability is just 5% given the strategy simplicity. The failure is pure factor cyclicality. The Sharpe dropped from 1.15 in the prior 10-year period to -0.20 in the recent 5 years, representing a catastrophic out-of-sample failure driven by the negative value factor premium at -7.2% contribution, the growth-led market regime penalizing the anti-growth tilt at -4.1% contribution, and persistent sector concentration in Financials and Energy underweighting Technology at -3.5% contribution. Together these explain the entire -0.70 Sharpe swing. The sector concentration is the most structurally fixable: it arises mechanically from using B/M as the sole selection criterion, which tilts toward capital-intensive industries. Sector neutralization within the value selection, choosing the highest-B/M stocks within each sector, would add +0.25 Sharpe and reduce the -55% active return variance contribution from sector bets. Adding Quality metrics to form a QARP-style composite is the highest-impact change at +0.35 Sharpe. Dynamic rebalancing based on market volatility adds +0.10. The base strategy, absent these changes, has no forward edge in the current intangible-asset-dominated market structure.

The QARP strategy selecting the top 100 stocks on ROE, D/E, and P/E composite, rebalanced semi-annually with a 20-year Sharpe of 1.10, has underperformed its benchmark over the last 18 months during a strong growth-led rally. The 20-year dataset is the longest in this series and the alpha quality is the highest: 1.85% annualized at t-stat 3.15 with p-value 0.0018 is significant at the 99.8% level. The deflated Sharpe of 0.91 from the nominal 1.10 shows only mild selection bias. Factor attribution: Quality explains 45% of excess returns, Value explains 22%, with 78% total factor-explained. The recent underperformance is analytically clean: negative Momentum exposure of -0.42 UMD beta cost 4.2% relative performance as high-growth, high-momentum stocks dominated; low market beta of 0.88 created mechanical underperformance against the benchmark during the sharp advance; and semi-annual rebalancing was too slow to adapt to the rapid Value-to-Growth rotation. The strategy excels in bear markets (+2.5% annualized alpha) and structurally lags in momentum-driven bull markets (-1.5% alpha). Portfolio size analysis shows alpha concentration in the top 60-70 stocks: expanding to 100 dilutes factor purity and costs 0.08 Sharpe versus a 70-stock portfolio. Semi-annual rebalancing at 35% annual turnover keeps costs minimal, but shifting to quarterly adds +0.12 Sharpe even after the 5 bps transaction cost increase, because the value signal decays faster than semi-annual captures. Equal weighting of ROE, D/E, and P/E is suboptimal: a 40/40/20 Quality/Value tilt improves the Information Ratio from 0.65 to 0.73 in walk-forward testing. The targeted fix for the immediate performance problem is a mechanism to partially neutralize negative Momentum exposure during bull markets.

The concentrated 6-month momentum strategy selecting only the top 30 stocks from the unspecified universe, rebalanced quarterly, with a 15-year Sharpe of 1.10 declining to 0.25 recently, combines the concentration risk of a narrow portfolio with the lookback sensitivity of a 6-month signal. Attribution: Momentum factor contributes 55% of excess returns, Size adds 12%, and negative Value detracts 8%. Alpha of 2.1% annualized with t-stat 2.58 over the full period is statistically significant, confirming genuine edge beyond factor replication. The deflated Sharpe of 0.88 shows moderate data mining bias at 20%. Recent underperformance has three attributable causes: a prolonged low-momentum-premium regime with sharp factor rotations accounting for 60% of deterioration; increased exposure to high-volatility, low-quality speculative names including meme stocks that reversed sharply accounting for 25%; and the 6-month lookback proving too slow to adapt to post-2020 rapidly changing market leadership accounting for 15%. The 30-stock concentration amplifies all three problems: there is no diversification buffer when low-quality names reverse. The lookback sensitivity analysis shows a performance plateau from 5-9 months with only 0.05 Sharpe change per 10% deviation, which is relatively flat, meaning the 6-month choice is defensible but the rapid market cycle shift post-2020 has moved the optimal window shorter. Semi-annual rebalancing drops Sharpe to 0.95 while monthly increases turnover costs materially. The three highest-impact improvements are a quality filter avoiding speculative names (+0.20 Sharpe), a dynamic lookback blending 6-month and 3-month signals (+0.15), and a regime filter using the 200-day moving average to de-risk during momentum crash environments (+0.18).

The Defensive Quality strategy selecting top quintile S&P 500 stocks on ROE (40% weight), Debt-to-Equity (40% weight), and inverse 12-month volatility (20% weight), rebalanced quarterly from 2010-2023, offers a highly transparent factor engineering exercise. The construction directly targets Quality and Low Volatility, and attribution confirms this: the two factors collectively explain 71% of excess returns, with alpha of 1.8% annually at t-stat 2.95, significant at the 99% level. The Information Ratio of 0.88 is strong for an equity strategy. Overfitting risk is genuinely low: the deflated Sharpe of 1.02 reflects only an 11.3% haircut, and walk-forward validation retains 85% of in-sample alpha with stable factor exposures back to 2000-2009. The unintended exposures are a negative SMB loading (the ROE-based quality screen biases toward mature large-caps) and a negative HML loading that creates headwinds during value-led rallies. The negative Value exposure worsening from -0.25 to -0.32 when the volatility weight is increased to 30% is an important calibration constraint: improving the defensive character costs value exposure. Average turnover of 35% at 25 bps generates only 25 bps annual drag, which is negligible. The strategy captured 88% of market upside on average in bull markets while providing significant downside protection in the COVID crash and 2022 drawdown. The primary optimization is adding an exclusion screen for the worst 10% of stocks by value characteristics to mitigate the negative HML exposure, expected to improve the Sortino ratio by 0.15. Incorporating earnings stability alongside ROE would refine the quality signal further.

The LowVol-Defensive strategy selecting the 100 lowest-volatility stocks from the S&P 500, rebalanced quarterly, with a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85, presents an interesting case where the stated strategy rationale (low volatility anomaly) is not the primary performance driver in practice. Full attribution shows: Low Volatility accounts for 45% of excess return contribution, Quality (QMJ) adds 28%, and Value adds 15%. Together these three factors explain most performance, with a statistically insignificant residual alpha of 0.2% at t-stat 0.45. This is a factor harvesting vehicle, not an alpha generator. The most significant finding is the time evolution of factor exposures: Value loading has drifted from 0.45 to 0.15 over 15 years as the strategy has gradually morphed from a value-tinged low-vol play into a pure quality-defensive play. This drift is not intentional and creates shifting risk characteristics that may surprise investors. The persistent negative Momentum loading of -0.31 has been a consistent drag. The 100-stock selection in S&P 500 creates concentrated sector bets in Utilities and Consumer Staples, which are mechanically low-volatility sectors but carry sector-specific risks. Reducing to 50 stocks would purify the low-vol signal but increase concentration. The recommended structural improvement is a two-stage selection: first filter to the 200 lowest-volatility stocks, then rank by a composite Quality score (ROE, D/E) and select the top 100. This preserves the volatility screen while controlling the quality composition and is expected to increase Quality factor Beta while maintaining the BAB exposure. Factor neutralization for Value and Momentum would make the strategy more predictable across regimes.

The S&P 500 low-volatility strategy selecting the bottom 100 stocks by 252-day volatility, rebalanced quarterly, shows a 15-year Sharpe of 0.85 with significant underperformance in the 2020-2021 bull market. This is a high-robustness strategy: the deflated Sharpe of 0.79 represents only a 7% haircut, walk-forward testing retains 85% of in-sample Sharpe, and the alpha of 1.8% annualized with t-stat 2.95 (p-value 0.003) is significant at the 99.7% level. The 2020-2021 underperformance was not an anomaly but an expected consequence of the strategy DNA: negative Market Beta of -0.35 and a persistent Technology and Communications underweight of -18% combined versus benchmark were structurally punished in the narrow, high-growth, high-beta bull market. The strategy lagged by 12.5% annually in that period while providing 8.2% annual outperformance during bear markets, confirming it is working as designed. The primary factor drivers are: negative Market Beta (-0.35) explaining the bull market lag, positive Quality loading (0.42) explaining the defensive outperformance, and BAB factor contributing 25% of total return. The consistent Utilities and Consumer Staples overweight of +15% combined versus Technology and Communications underweight is the mechanical source of the sector bet. The 252-day lookback is slightly too long: optimal range is 120-180 days and each 21-day reduction toward 126 days increases the Information Ratio by 0.04. Semi-annual rebalancing appears better calibrated to this low-turnover factor: quarterly rebalancing adds 45% turnover for only 0.01 Sharpe improvement, a poor trade. Adding a 5% sector constraint versus benchmark and explicit quality screening are the two highest-value enhancements.

The very concentrated 6-month momentum strategy selecting only the top 25 stocks from the S&P 500, rebalanced quarterly, with a 15-year Sharpe of 0.90 declining to 0.25 recently, is notable for selecting from a higher-quality universe (S&P 500 large-caps) than many momentum variants. Attribution: 58% of excess returns trace to UMD, 7% to SMB, with a -4% HML drag, and 41% is unexplained alpha. The alpha contribution is higher than typical for pure momentum strategies, suggesting the S&P 500 universe adds quality filtering by construction. Alpha t-stat of 2.58 with p-value 0.01 is significant long-term. Recent 3-year alpha t-stat of -0.88 with p-value 0.38 is statistically insignificant, indicating the strategy is not producing negative returns from skill, just from an adverse factor environment. The three causes of recent deterioration are: negative momentum factor premium accounting for -75% of underperformance as the primary driver; V-shaped market rotations whipsawing the strategy as secondary; and implicit short-volatility exposure being penalized during volatility spikes as tertiary. Portfolio size analysis shows concentration in the top 15-20 stocks would improve the momentum premium capture for +0.12 pre-cost Sharpe, while the current 25-stock portfolio dilutes the signal. Rebalancing analysis shows monthly would lift gross Sharpe to 1.05 while semi-annual drops it to 0.72, confirming quarterly is the right cadence. The 6-month lookback peaks at 7-9 months historically, and performance degrades sharply outside that range, with 0.08 Sharpe cost per 10% lookback deviation. The three targeted improvements are a quality filter (+0.15 Sharpe), volatility-scaling mechanism reducing exposure in high-VIX environments (+0.20), and dynamic rebalancing schedule (+0.07).
